items.title: Frank Foster interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 7, 1998
items.q: Around August of 1945 I heard “Now is the Time” and “Billie’s Bounce” for the first time, and Charlie Parker for the first time. And from that moment forward, it was all over, I was a confirmed bebopper.

ctx.x: And this was like, as you described before, like it snatched you.

Around August of 1945 I heard “Now is the Time” and “Billie’s Bounce” for the first time, and Charlie Parker for the first time. And from that moment forward, it was all over, I was a confirmed bebopper. And the idols that I had worshipped up to that time — Johnny Hodges, Willie Smith and Benny Carter — sort of fell by the wayside. And it wasn’t until years later when I was already in my 20s that I looked back and began to appreciate about what I had originally liked about them, because as one matures one…
Yeah. You don’t have to replace the old with the new. You can listen to both of them.

items.title: Frank Foster and Bill Hughes interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Schenectady, New York, March 28, 1995
items.q: I’m so ashamed that I don’t remember the show Bird was on.

ctx.x: Well that was the thing from those days, you know, guys would purposely, you know, go out looking for a session, for one particular guy, for the cutting contests. That doesn’t happen much anymore, but I mean they would take it through all sorts of things I suppose, you know, changing keys, and tunes and if you couldn’t hang, you were dead. But I remember this one particular instance, we were doing a Birdland show. And I don’t remember, I remember we flew up to Boston and we did the show, and then we flew right…
I’m so ashamed that I don’t remember the show Bird was on.

Bird came up, unfortunately Bird didn’t have a horn when he came up. So Bird borrowed the horn from, I think he borrowed Ernie Wilkins’ horn, and it was something terribly out of whack with the reed as far as Bird was concerned, that Ernie was using. So every other note that Bird played that night was a squeak, you know? And I just remember being, you know, like oh my goodness, Bird. But he shot through it like he didn’t, you know—

items.title: Frank Foster — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: She took me to Birdland and persuaded Charlie Parker to allow me to sit in.

ctx.x: This is some inside stuff [laughs]. Yes, she’s a good singer. She let me know that Bird was coming to town. She was practically a Bird groupie [laughs], if such a term can be applied. I think we were together. We went to hear Bird. I of course had heard his recordings and was happily impressed with his live appearance. I was also

impressed with his microphone technique. He was on the same program with Ruth Brown. I found out that he could speak as well as he could perform on the instrument, and I gained a new respect for him then. My next experience with Bird was my first night in New York City to join the Count Basie orchestra, Monday, July 27, 1953. I don’t remember too many dates. I remember the day, the date and the year.
